h1: The Miami Restaurant Marketing Calendar: What to Promote Every Month
metaTitle: Miami Restaurant Marketing Calendar: Ideas by Month
metaDescription: A month-by-month restaurant marketing calendar for Miami owners. What to promote and simple content and offer ideas for every season, in plain English.
heroAlt: A sunny Miami street with palm trees and outdoor restaurant tables
directAnswer: A restaurant marketing calendar is a simple month-by-month plan of what to promote and post, matched to what is actually happening in Miami. intro:
You are wiping down the counter on a slow Tuesday night, you open Instagram to post something, and your mind goes blank. What do you even say? By the time you think of something, the night is over. Most owners market in these panicked little bursts, with no plan behind it.

There is a calmer way, and it does not take a marketing degree. It is called a marketing calendar, which is just a simple plan of what to promote each month, lined up with what is already happening in your city. Valentine's Day, Calle Ocho, Miami Spice, the holidays. Miami hands you a reason to post, and a reason for people to come in, almost every month.

This guide walks you through the whole year, month by month, in plain English. For each stretch I will tell you what is happening in Miami, what to promote, and one or two concrete ideas you can run. At the end I will show you, click by click, how to turn it into a habit that takes about an hour a month.

sections.h2: Why a marketing calendar beats scrambling every week
sections.html:
Before we get into the months, let us define a few words so nothing trips you up.

  • A promotion is anything you push to get people in the door: a special dish, a holiday menu, a discount, an event. To promote it just means to tell people about it.
  • A post is a photo, video, or few lines you put on Instagram, Facebook, or your Google listing.
  • An offer is a specific deal with a clear reason and end date, like a Mother's Day brunch or a special price on stone crab.

The most useful thing to understand about marketing in Miami is that the city runs on two speeds. From December to April it is high season. Tourists fill the hotels, snowbirds (people who live up north and spend the winter here) come back, and money is in town. From roughly June to November it is slow season: hotter, quieter, and inside hurricane season. Your job is not to fight this rhythm, it is to ride it. Compete for visitors in high season; take care of your locals in the slow months. The whole calendar below is built on that one idea.

sections.h2: January and February: high season, Valentine's, and the food festival
sections.html:
January: fresh starts and full tables

January is quietly one of your best months. High season is in full swing and Miami is packed with visitors escaping the cold. It is also when people swear they will eat better, so fresh sells, and stone crab (Florida's iconic winter catch, in season from mid-October to early May) is at its best.

What to promote: a light, fresh dish for the new-year crowd, your stone crab, and cozy dinners for the tourists in town.

Ideas to run:

  • Post a short video of a fresh, colorful dish captioned "New year, same fresh ingredients." Tag your neighborhood, whether Brickell, Wynwood, or Coral Gables, so nearby visitors find you.
  • Run a "Dry January" mocktail (a cocktail with no alcohol) for the crowd taking a break from drinking. It costs little and gets talked about.

February: the busiest, most romantic month

February is peak season and full of reasons to eat out. Valentine's Day falls on Saturday, February 14 in 2026, the best possible day for it, and the South Beach Wine and Food Festival (a huge four-day food event, February 19 to 22 in 2026) brings food-obsessed crowds to town.

What to promote: Valentine's reservations first, then anything that rides the food-festival buzz.

Ideas to run:

  • Announce a Valentine's set menu (a fixed list of courses for one price, also called a prix-fixe) two to three weeks early and tell people to reserve. Romance sells out, so start by late January.
  • During festival week, post a "if you love food this week, come find us" special to reach visitors browsing where to eat.

sections.h2: March and April: Calle Ocho, spring break, and the last of high season
sections.html:
March: Carnaval, Calle Ocho, and spring break

March is loud, busy, and very Miami. Carnaval Miami builds through the first half of the month and peaks with the Calle Ocho street festival, the largest Hispanic street party in the country, on Sunday, March 15 in 2026, in the heart of Little Havana. Spring break brings a young, hungry crowd, and it is still high season.

What to promote: your Latin and Caribbean dishes, festival energy, and quick, shareable food for spring break.

Ideas to run:

  • If you are in or near Little Havana, run a Calle Ocho weekend special a week ahead. Even out in Doral or Hialeah, lean into the Latin pride of the season with a featured dish and its story.
  • Post a high-energy Reel (a short vertical video on Instagram) of your most colorful plate or drink. Spring break crowds share what looks good.

April: catch the last of the visitors

April is the handoff month. High season winds down toward the end of it, your last easy stretch of tourist traffic before the quiet sets in. Easter and Passover bring family meals.

What to promote: an Easter brunch or family meal, and a gentle "before summer" push to catch the visitors still here.

Ideas to run:

  • Offer an Easter Sunday brunch or family-style meal and take reservations. Families plan ahead, so promote about two weeks out.
  • Start collecting follows and emails now (a "follow us for summer specials" card on the table) so you can reach these guests when things slow down.

sections.h2: May and June: Mother's Day, Father's Day, and the World Cup kicks off
sections.html:
May: Mother's Day is the main event

May is the bridge into slow season. The rush eases, but May hands you the biggest restaurant day of the year: Mother's Day, Sunday, May 10 in 2026, when more families eat out than almost any other day. Stone crab season closes on May 1, so feature it in the final days. Cinco de Mayo, graduations, and Memorial Day weekend round out the month.

What to promote: Mother's Day above all, then graduation gatherings and Memorial Day.

Ideas to run:

  • Promote a Mother's Day brunch or dinner hard, starting in late April, with reservations, a special dish for moms, or a free dessert. This is worth more than any other single promotion all year.
  • Post a "book your graduation dinner" message aimed at local families across Miami-Dade.

June: Father's Day and a World Cup summer

June begins the slow, hot season, and hurricane season officially opens on June 1 (running through November 30). But 2026 is no ordinary summer: the FIFA World Cup comes to Hard Rock Stadium, with Miami matches on June 15, 21, 24, and 27 and more games deep into July, a rare summer reason for people to go out. Father's Day lands on Sunday, June 21.

What to promote: World Cup watch parties, Father's Day, and your air conditioning (comfort matters when it is 92 degrees out).

Ideas to run:

  • Host a World Cup watch party on the big match days. Post the schedule, promise the games on your screens, and add a game-day food or drink special.
  • Run a Father's Day deal aimed at dads (a hearty plate, a beer pairing) and take reservations a week ahead.

sections.h2: July and August: the slow heat, the Semiquincentennial, and Miami Spice
sections.html:
July: the 250th of July

July is hot and, once the World Cup crowds thin out, genuinely slow. But it opens with a bang: July 4, 2026 is a Saturday and America's 250th birthday (the Semiquincentennial, a once-in-a-lifetime anniversary), so expect a bigger, longer celebration than a normal Fourth. The World Cup knockout rounds also run into mid-July at Hard Rock Stadium.

What to promote: a July 4 celebration built around the 250th, then comfort and value for locals.

Ideas to run:

  • Do something special for the 250th of July: a red, white, and blue dish or drink, a cookout menu, or a fireworks view if you have one. Promote two weeks ahead.
  • For the rest of the month, run a locals' weekday special to keep tables full when tourists are gone, like "Miami locals get 15 percent off Monday to Thursday."

August: the quietest month, so take care of locals

August is the hottest and usually slowest month in Miami. It is also when Miami Spice begins, a citywide program (August 1 through September 30 in 2026) where restaurants offer discounted fixed-price menus to pull diners out during the slow season.

What to promote: your Miami Spice menu if you join, or your own slow-season value deal, plus family meals for back-to-school.

Ideas to run:

  • Consider joining Miami Spice, or run your own version: a three-course menu at one fair price. Post it clearly and repeat weekly through September.
  • Offer a back-to-school family meal (kids eat free, or a family bundle) for tired parents in your neighborhood.

sections.h2: September and October: Hispanic Heritage Month and the return of stone crab
sections.html:
September: Miami Spice and Hispanic heritage

September is still hot, still slow, and the peak of hurricane season, so keep plans flexible. Miami Spice continues all month, and Hispanic Heritage Month runs September 15 to October 15, which means a lot in a city as Latin as Miami.

What to promote: your Miami Spice menu, and a Hispanic Heritage feature done with real heart.

Ideas to run:

  • Feature a heritage dish and tell its story: where it comes from, who in your family made it. In neighborhoods like Little Havana, Hialeah, or Doral this connects deeply. Post it in English and Spanish.
  • Keep reposting your Miami Spice or value menu; September diners are hunting for deals.

October: stone crab is back and the city wakes up

October is when Miami starts to stir again. The heat begins to break, and stone crab season reopens on October 15, a real event for seafood lovers here. Hispanic Heritage Month runs to October 15, and Halloween closes the month.

What to promote: the return of stone crab, a Halloween moment, and the first hints of high season coming back.

Ideas to run:

  • If you serve seafood, make a loud deal about stone crab being back on October 15. Post it that morning. Regulars wait all summer for this.
  • Run a simple Halloween special: a themed drink, a costume discount, or a family early-evening deal.

sections.h2: November and December: the holiday rush, Art Basel, and Noche Buena
sections.html:
November: high season returns with Thanksgiving

November flips the switch back to high season. The snowbirds return, the weather turns beautiful, and the holidays begin. Thanksgiving falls on Thursday, November 26 in 2026, and many families want the meal without the cooking, which is an opening for you. Small Business Saturday, the day after, is a great day for a locally owned spot to be loud.

What to promote: Thanksgiving dining or takeout, holiday party bookings, and gift cards.

Ideas to run:

  • Offer a Thanksgiving meal, either dine-in reservations or a take-home feast families can reheat. Start promoting in early November, because people plan ahead.
  • Open your books for holiday parties now. Post "now booking December holiday parties" and make it easy for offices and families in Brickell or Coral Gables to reserve.

December: your biggest, busiest month

December is the peak of the year, and everything happens at once. Art Basel and Miami Art Week (the main fair runs December 4 to 6 in 2026) flood the city with a wealthy, international crowd, especially around Miami Beach and Wynwood. Noche Buena (Christmas Eve, December 24) is one of the biggest nights of the year for Miami's Cuban and Latin families, built around a huge home feast, and Christmas and New Year's Eve close things out.

What to promote: holiday celebrations, Noche Buena, and a New Year's Eve plan, all booked in advance.

Ideas to run:

  • During Art Basel week, post polished photos and a special aimed at visitors. If you are near Wynwood or Miami Beach, mention the art crowd directly.
  • Lean hard into Noche Buena: offer a family feast, a roast pork (lechon) to go, or catering trays for people hosting at home. Promote from early December, because this night sells out.
  • Sell a New Year's Eve plan and open bookings by mid-December.

sections.h2: How do you actually use this calendar every month?
sections.html:
A calendar only helps if you use it. Staying ahead takes about an hour a month, done in one sitting.

Step 1: Set a monthly planning hour

  1. Open your calendar app (on an iPhone it is the Calendar app; on Android it is Google Calendar).
  2. Create a new event on the 25th of each month called "Plan next month's promos."
  3. Set it to repeat monthly so it comes back on its own. Give yourself one hour.

In that hour, look at the month coming up, pick your promotions, and decide on your posts and offers. One or two solid ideas per month is plenty.

Step 2: Decide one promotion and one offer per moment

For each holiday or event that month, write down two things: what you will promote and one offer or post to go with it. A finished, simple plan beats a fancy one you never run.

Step 3: Schedule your posts for free, all at once

You do not have to post live every day. You can write your posts once and let them publish themselves for free using Meta Business Suite, the tool from Instagram and Facebook's parent company for managing both accounts. Here is how, on a computer:

  1. Go to business.facebook.com in your web browser and sign in with the Facebook account linked to your restaurant's page.
  2. Make sure your Instagram account is connected to that page (the site will prompt you if it is not).
  3. Click Create post, usually near the top left.
  4. Under Post to, choose your Facebook page and your Instagram account so one post goes to both.
  5. Add your photo or video, then write your caption, including what the food is and your neighborhood.
  6. Turn on the Set date and time option (sometimes labeled Schedule) and pick when it should go live.
  7. Click Schedule. Repeat for the other posts you planned.

Now your feed stays alive even during a brutal week on the floor, because you did the work once. You can schedule about 75 days ahead, so a single sitting covers weeks.

faqs.q: What is a restaurant marketing calendar?
faqs.a: A restaurant marketing calendar is a simple month-by-month plan of what you will promote and post, matched to what is happening in your city and on the holiday calendar. Instead of scrambling for an idea each week, you decide in advance that, for example, February is for Valentine's reservations and August is for a slow-season value menu. It keeps your marketing steady and tied to the moments when people actually want to go out.

faqs.q: What should a Miami restaurant promote in the slow summer months?
faqs.a: In Miami's slow summer, roughly June through September when it is hot and tourists thin out, focus on locals rather than visitors. Run weekday specials, family and back-to-school deals, and value menus like Miami Spice, which runs August through September. In 2026, the World Cup at Hard Rock Stadium in June and July, plus the July 4 celebrations, are rare summer traffic boosters worth building watch parties and specials around.

faqs.q: When is Miami's high season for restaurants?
faqs.a: Miami's high season runs from about December to April. Cooler weather up north sends tourists and seasonal residents, known as snowbirds, to the city, hotels fill up, and people spend more freely. This is the time to promote holiday dinners, Valentine's Day, reservations, and higher-end specials with confidence, because demand is at its yearly peak.

faqs.q: What are the biggest Miami events to plan my promotions around?
faqs.a: The standout Miami moments are Art Basel and Miami Art Week in early December, Noche Buena on December 24, the South Beach Wine and Food Festival in February, Calle Ocho and Carnaval Miami in March, and Miami Spice across August and September. Around these, add the major US holidays like Valentine's Day, Mother's Day, Father's Day, July 4, Thanksgiving, and New Year's Eve. Each one is a built-in reason to run a promotion.

faqs.q: How far in advance should I promote a holiday special?
faqs.a: For a big reservation-driven day like Valentine's Day, Mother's Day, Thanksgiving, or New Year's Eve, start promoting two to three weeks ahead, because people plan those meals early and popular time slots sell out. For smaller, walk-in moments like a Halloween drink or a weekday special, a few days of notice is enough. A good rule: the bigger the day, the earlier you start.

faqs.q: Do I need to pay for tools to schedule my restaurant's posts?
faqs.a: No. Meta Business Suite is free and lets you write and schedule posts for both Instagram and Facebook from one place. You sign in at business.facebook.com with your restaurant's Facebook page, click Create post, add your photo and caption, turn on the schedule option, pick a date and time, and click Schedule. You can plan weeks of posts in a single sitting at no cost.

faqs.q: I run a small place by myself. Is a marketing calendar really worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is built for exactly that situation. A calendar means you make your marketing decisions once a month in about an hour, then schedule the posts and forget them, instead of losing energy to it every single day. For a small, independent spot, that saved time and steadier presence is the whole point. If it still feels like too much, handing it to a social media partner is a common and reasonable choice.
